html:
SMTO-SSH-0001 — SMTO stopped because a remote computer's identity changed

GUID: b21f7f8f-6748-469d-a2db-bc87d9872cc3
Slug: ssh-host-identity-changed
Domain: SSH · Subsystem: ssh

What happened

  • When SMTO connected to the other computer over SSH, its security key didn't match the one SMTO trusts, or the saved key couldn't be read. SMTO stopped rather than log in to a computer it can't confirm.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Ask the person who manages that remote computer whether it was recently rebuilt, reinstalled, replaced or given a new address. Those changes give a computer a new security key, which is the harmless explanation for this message.
  2. If nobody expected the change, don't connect again. Tell that person right away. An unexpected key change can mean you're reaching the wrong computer, so sending passwords or commands there isn't safe.
  3. If the change is expected, ask the person who manages the Gateway computer (the computer SMTO uses to run commands) to confirm the new key and update its trusted-computers list. SSH only accepts a new key after someone confirms it with the remote computer's manager and replaces the old entry on purpose; SMTO never accepts a changed key by itself.
  4. After the trusted entry is updated, start a new conversation by typing /new and ask SMTO to run the command there. This conversation still remembers the old key and will keep refusing the computer, while a new conversation learns the confirmed key.

What success looks like

  • The command runs on the remote computer and its output appears in the conversation without an identity warning.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages the Gateway computer. Don't turn off SSH's key checking, and don't accept the new key until someone has confirmed it.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • OpenSSH or SMTO's host-key check found that the remote computer's host key is malformed, conflicts with another pinned key, or differs from the key trusted earlier.

What this means

  • SSH identity validation could not establish one acceptable trusted host key. This identity includes malformed fingerprint input, contradictory pinned evidence and an observed key change. A replaced server and an unexpected endpoint are different explanations; neither should be assumed without verification.

Why this can happen

  • The saved fingerprint may be malformed, retained identity evidence may conflict, or SSH may report a changed host key.

How to diagnose it

  • Use the bounded technical detail to distinguish invalid fingerprint syntax from a conflicting or changed key. For a change, verify the host-key fingerprint with the server administrator through an independent trusted channel.

How to fix it

  • OpenSSH reported 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED', or the pinned or saved fingerprint did not match the key. Verify the new host-key fingerprint through an independent trusted channel (for example ssh-keygen -lf on the remote's /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key.pub), then remove the old entry on the Gateway account with ssh-keygen -R and the host name and add the verified key. Conversation-scoped SSH pins keep the old key, so re-enroll from a new conversation; never disable host-key checking.
  • Verify the host key through a trusted channel before explicitly updating the supported known-hosts configuration. Never automatically accept a changed host key.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • Confirm the observed host-key fingerprint matches the identity verified through an independent trusted channel before reconnecting.

What not to do

  • Do not automatically accept a changed key or disable SSH host-key checking.

Technical notes

  • This identity covers an invalid saved fingerprint, conflicting pinned evidence and an observed changed host key; not every occurrence proves the server changed.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
